sub.en: Look at the sentences. Which word do you use for a person, which for a thing, and which for a place?

items.q: She’s the woman ___ cleans our street.
items.why: who for people, which for things, where for places. that works for people and things, but not for places.

items.q: It’s the machine ___ heats your food in two minutes.
That’s the room ___ we keep everything we never use.
It’s a thing ___ you use for washing the floor.
The house ___ we’re staying is huge.
I love the candles ___ they keep in the bathroom.
It’s the cupboard ___ clothes hang.
items.why: The inside of a cupboard is a place, so where — even though a cupboard is also a thing.

items.q: He’s the man ___ sells tea on the corner.

acts.title: The house we’re looking after
text: We are house-sitting for a family who are in Canada for three months, and the house is full of things we don’t have names for.

There is a machine in the kitchen which does something to vegetables — it has eleven buttons and no instructions. Next to it is the thing that heats food in two minutes, which at least we recognise. There is no proper cooker. In a house where somebody clearly cooks a great deal, that is strange.

Upstairs there is a cupboard where the clothes hang, and beside it the low one with the drawers you pull out. Neither of us can remember the word for the second one. The bed has sheets which feel like a hotel’s and a duvet so thick that we can’t close the wardrobe door on it.
The bathroom is where the candles are, about thirty of them, and the towels are the kind that hotels take back off you.
The one thing we understand completely is the dustpan and brush by the back door. That’s the thing you use when you have broken something. We have used it twice.

items.q: The writers are
The machine with eleven buttons
What the kitchen does NOT have:
They can’t remember the word for
The bathroom contains about thirty
What have they used the dustpan and brush for?

items.q: The relative word the writer uses for a thing.
items.a: which

items.q: The relative word the writer uses for a place.
items.a: where

items.q: The word for the tall cupboard where clothes hang.
items.a: wardrobe

items.q: The word for the thick thing you sleep under.
items.a: duvet

tts: The house where we’re staying is huge. I suppose they always say things are much bigger in the States, don’t they?
They have some beautiful things. I love all the candles in the bathroom and the soft, white towels — oh, and the Egyptian cotton sheets on the bed are wonderful!
It’s a really lovely place, but I’m still missing certain things from home, such as my own bed and even my duvet!
Also, one thing which I don’t like — they don’t have a proper cooker, just a microwave oven. Hard to believe in such a big place.

items.s: She likes the candles in the bathroom.
The house has a proper cooker.
The house has a microwave oven.

lines.s: I don’t know the word either. It’s a ___ you use in the kitchen. 🍳
Ah — a microwave. And the tall cupboard?

A wardrobe. And the woman outside?
She’s the ___ who cleans our street. 🧹

write.q: Look around the room you are in and define five things without naming them: two with which or that, one with who, one with where, and one with “It’s used for…”.
write.model: It’s a thing which you turn to get water — I mean the tap. It’s the machine that heats food in two minutes. She’s the person who brings the post every morning. That’s the cupboard where I keep everything I never use. And this small one is used for picking up broken glass — a dustpan, I think.

speak.q: Choose four objects near you and define each one out loud without saying its name. Use who, which, where and “It’s used for…” once each.
speak.model: It’s a thing which you sleep under. It’s the place where you hang your clothes. He’s the man who cleans our street. This is used for drying your hands.
